Right, Wrong, or Unfinished: A Competing Risks Framework for Language-Model Reasoning under Token Budgets

Boen Jiang    Guanhua Fang    Wen Yu Affiliation: Department of Statistics and Data Science, Fudan University
Abstract

Assessing language-model performance under a token budget requires understanding both when a response will finish and whether it will be correct. We develop Competing Risks Analysis of Token Expenditure in Reasoning (CRATER), a statistically principled framework that treats correct and incorrect completion as distinct competing event types and responses unfinished at the generation limit as administratively right-censored. The fitted distribution provides probabilities of correct completion, incorrect completion, and remaining unfinished across token budgets, together with expected token consumption. We evaluate the proposed method using responses to MATH questions and demonstrate its value in two downstream applications. For routing before generation, CRATER guides the joint choice of a model configuration and token budget. Under hypothetical token prices, it reduces mean cost by 53.39% relative to a strong reference, with observed correct-completion rates of 96.42% and 97.30%, respectively. For repeated sampling, we combine CRATER’s single-attempt success probabilities with an existing beta-binomial calibration approach to predict pass@kk. Across both applications, CRATER delivers predictions at any specified token budget up to the generation limit from a common model of completion time and correctness, eliminating the need for separate parameter estimation for each budget.

Keywords: Competing risks, Censoring, Prediction calibration, Computational budget

1 Introduction

The usefulness of a language-model response depends on both its content and the resources required to produce it. Practical applications therefore require attention to the cost of obtaining a successful response as well as the probability of success. For example, FrugalGPT studies this trade-off in news classification, reading comprehension, and scientific question answering, showing that adaptive use of models can reduce expenditure while maintaining task accuracy (Chen et al. 2024b). In mathematical reasoning, Snell et al. (2025) show that the effective allocation of inference-time computation depends on problem difficulty. These examples motivate decisions about which model to use, how long to let it generate, and how many attempts to allow. Such decisions benefit from predictions of both the probability of obtaining a correct answer within a specified budget and the resources that generation would consume.

Using predicted success probabilities to guide resource allocation requires understanding how well they reflect observed outcomes. Calibration, which asks whether predicted probabilities of correctness agree with observed frequencies, forms part of the broader statistical study of uncertainty in language-model outputs (Ji et al. 2025; Tian et al. 2023). Kadavath et al. (2022) study probabilities that a proposed answer is correct and that a model can answer a question correctly before a particular answer is given. Tian et al. (2023) find that elicited verbal confidence can be better calibrated than model probabilities on question-answering benchmarks. For resource allocation, these assessments of correctness must be considered together with the computation required to obtain a response. The relevant prediction is then the probability of correct completion within a specified budget, together with the expected resources consumed.

Output-length modeling addresses the resource component of this problem. For interactive serving, Qiu et al. (2024) predict output sequence lengths from input queries using a lightweight proxy model and use these predictions to prioritize shorter requests, reducing average request completion times and improving throughput. During generation, Piotrowski et al. (2025) use hidden states from multiple transformer layers to predict the number of tokens remaining in a response. Moving from length predictions to distributional modeling, Zheng et al. (2026) fit log-tt distributions to output lengths and use information about their tails to improve scheduling for online inference and offline data generation. Model routing uses predictions of response quality and cost to guide model selection. CARROT estimates both quantities conditional on the input question, while R2-Router jointly selects a model and an output-length budget (Somerstep et al. 2025; Xue et al. 2026). Together, these studies motivate probability assessments that account for both response quality and resource consumption. Our focus is a joint distribution that connects completion length to correctness, so that success probabilities and expected consumption at different budgets arise from a common statistical model.

At any token budget, a response can have completed correctly, completed incorrectly, or remain unfinished. Distinguishing these states matters because accuracy among completed responses conditions on a population that changes with the budget, while an unfinished response has an unknown eventual outcome. If observation stops at a generation limit before completion is recorded, its completion time is administratively right-censored. Nagpal (2025) applies the Kaplan-Meier estimator to language-model generation lengths under right censoring. To incorporate correctness, we treat correct and incorrect completion as two competing event types, with unfinished responses remaining at risk. The competing-risks framework relates their cause-specific hazards to the probabilities of correct completion, incorrect completion, and no completion by each budget (Putter et al. 2007). It thus retains information from capped responses while allowing the timing of the two completion types to differ. The target is the joint behavior of completion time and outcome within the observed token window, conditional on question information available before generation.

We propose Competing Risks Analysis of Token Expenditure in Reasoning (CRATER), a competing-risks based working model on the output-token scale. CRATER combines question-embedding features with configuration- and cause-specific time effects, using both completed and administratively censored responses for estimation. The fitted distribution yields probabilities of correct completion, incorrect completion, and remaining unfinished, together with expected token consumption, across budgets within the observation window. We study CRATER using language-model responses to MATH questions (Hendrycks et al. 2021).

We illustrate the value of the fitted distribution in two downstream tasks. (i) For routing, predicted success probabilities and expected consumption guide the choice of a configuration and token budget before generation. Under the primary hypothetical prices, the CRATER-based routers achieve lower mean cost than nearest-neighbor predictors using the corresponding question representations, with similar observed correct-completion rates; the magnitude of savings depends on the price assumptions. (ii) For repeated sampling, the model supplies budget-specific probabilities for predicting whether at least one of kk attempts succeeds, the quantity summarized by pass@kk (Chen et al. 2021). We connect these predictions to a beta-binomial model, following Kazdan et al. (2025), to adjust the predicted mean and account for residual variation in success probabilities when calculating repeated-sampling success. This adjustment improves agreement with average empirical pass@kk in the reported comparisons, which cover up to ten attempts per question. Both applications use the same underlying description of completion time and correctness. Figure 1 summarizes the framework. Our contributions are threefold.

  1. 1.

    We formulate budget-constrained language-model reasoning as a competing-risks problem, jointly describing completion length and correctness while retaining information from responses right-censored at the generation limit.

  2. 2.

    We develop CRATER, a conditional working model combining question-embedding features with configuration- and cause-specific time adjustments. We estimate the model by penalized likelihood, using a slope-fusion penalty to control the complexity of the time adjustments.

  3. 3.

    We apply CRATER to model-budget routing and repeated-sampling prediction using MATH responses. Both applications obtain predictions at any specified token budget within the observation window from the same fitted distribution, without refitting the completion model for each budget.

The Python implementation of CRATER and scripts for reproducing the reported analyses are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/llm-competing-risks-4463.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 defines the observations and introduces the data. Section 3 presents the CRATER working model and estimation procedure. Section 4 reports parameter estimates, model fit, and component ablations. Section 5 develops the routing and repeated-sampling applications, followed by a discussion of limitations and further directions in Section 6.

2 Problem setup and dataset

2.1 Budgeted reasoning tasks

A budgeted reasoning task asks a language model to answer a question using a limited number of output tokens. We call the output from one generation attempt “a response sample", or simply “a sample". It may contain intermediate reasoning as well as a proposed final answer. Generation stops when the model finishes or its token allowance is exhausted. A completed response can be correct or incorrect under a task-specific assessment rule, while an interrupted response may have no final answer. The outcome therefore depends on both the time required to complete the response and the correctness of that completion.

A generation experiment combines a collection of questions, a set of model configurations, a stopping rule, and an assessment procedure. A configuration specifies the model and the conditions under which it generates responses, including prompting and decoding settings. Repeated sampling for the same question under the same configuration can produce different texts, completion times, and answers. Output-token count provides an observable measure of generation length; its relationship to computation, latency or price also depends on the configuration and serving environment.

Let ii index questions, mm model configurations and rr repeated response samples. The question text qiq_{i} includes the problem statement and any task context available before generation. For the response sample (i,m,r)(i,m,r), let Ti​m​rT_{imr} be the natural completion time measured in output tokens, and let Ji​m​r=1J_{imr}=1 or 22 indicate whether the completed response is correct or incorrect according to the assessment rule.

With a prespecified token cap Ci​m​rC_{imr}, we observe the recorded length T~i​m​r=min⁡(Ti​m​r,Ci​m​r)\widetilde{T}_{imr}=\min(T_{imr},C_{imr}) and the event indicator

Δi​m​r={1,Ti​m​r≤Ci​m​r,Ji​m​r=1(correct completion),2,Ti​m​r≤Ci​m​r,Ji​m​r=2(incorrect completion),0,Ti​m​r>Ci​m​r(right censoring).\Delta_{imr}=\begin{cases}1,&T_{imr}\leq C_{imr},\ J_{imr}=1\quad\text{(correct completion)},\\ 2,&T_{imr}\leq C_{imr},\ J_{imr}=2\quad\text{(incorrect completion)},\\ 0,&T_{imr}>C_{imr}\quad\text{(right censoring)}.\end{cases} (1)

Thus correctness is recorded only for responses completed before the cap. Response samples reaching the cap remain in the dataset as administratively right-censored records, with natural completion time and eventual correctness unobserved. The strict pre-cap convention reflects the available records, which do not distinguish natural completion exactly at the cap from stopping at the generation limit; Appendix A gives the generation and scoring details.

The observed data form the indexed collection

𝒟text={(qi,m,Ci​m​r,T~i​m​r,Δi​m​r)}(i,m,r)∈ℐ,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{text}}=\bigl\{(q_{i},m,C_{imr},\widetilde{T}_{imr},\Delta_{imr})\bigr\}_{(i,m,r)\in\mathcal{I}}, (2)

where ℐ\mathcal{I} indexes the question–configuration–sample combinations present in the experiment. Each record contains the question text, model configuration, token cap, recorded length and event code. The indices ii and rr organize the observations rather than constitute data fields. The same qiq_{i} is shared across configurations and repetitions, while the cap, length and event code refer to an individual response sample. Generated responses, reference answers and assessment records support the construction and checking of the outcomes. They need not be available to a prediction rule applied before generation. Questions provide the natural grouping unit when the aim is to predict performance on other questions, so their repeated observations should remain together in training and evaluation partitions.

For a prospective budget BB, the prediction targets are the probabilities of correct completion, incorrect completion, and no completion by BB, conditional on the question and configuration. The probability of a correct completion per response sample combines the chance of finishing with the conditional correctness on finishing. A point estimate of response length or an accuracy calculated only among completed responses describes only part of this problem. Budget-indexed probabilities can inform which configuration to invoke, how many tokens to allocate and how to assess the potential benefit of repeated sampling. Learning these probabilities across questions requires a numerical representation of the question information available before generation.

2.2 Representing questions with embeddings

Question text contains information about the task to be solved, but its variable length and symbolic content do not directly form a fixed set of numerical covariates. A text embedding supplies such a representation. Let ee be a fixed encoder and define

zi=e⁡(qi)=(zi​1,…,zi​d)⊤∈ℝd.z_{i}=e(q_{i})=\bigl(z_{i1},\ldots,z_{id}\bigr)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (3)

The encoder maps each question to a vector of the same dimension, allowing statistical models to relate variation in question content to observed completion and correctness. Its coordinates jointly represent aspects of the text; an individual coordinate need not have a direct interpretation as difficulty or a particular reasoning ability.

Representative text encoders include Sentence-BERT, E5 and the BGE family. Sentence-BERT adapts BERT to produce sentence vectors that can be compared through cosine similarity (Reimers and Gurevych 2019). E5 learns general-purpose text representations through contrastive pretraining on large collections of weakly supervised text pairs (Wang et al. 2022). BGE-M3 supports multilingual embedding across input lengths ranging from short sentences to longer documents (Chen et al. 2024a). These models provide different implementations of the text-to-vector map, with different training objectives and input capabilities.

Embedding encoders can also be built from generative language models. Qwen3 Embedding uses Qwen3 foundation models as its backbone and combines large-scale pretraining with supervised fine-tuning for text representation (Zhang et al. 2025). The family provides multilingual embedding models at several parameter scales, including an 8B variant. The encoder and covariate construction used in our analysis are described in Section 3.2.

Since the encoder receives the question before a response is generated, the same ziz_{i} is available for all configurations and response samples associated with qiq_{i}. Replacing qiq_{i} by ziz_{i} in (2) gives a numerical data structure consisting of question vectors, configuration identifiers, token caps, recorded lengths and event indicators. A new question can be encoded in the same way before selecting a model or allocating its budget. The input to this representation is the question text, without its generated response, reference solution or observed correctness.

2.3 Budgeted reasoning on MATH dataset

MATH is a benchmark for evaluating mathematical problem solving, containing 12,500 problems from mathematics competitions such as the AMC 10, AMC 12 and AIME (Hendrycks et al. 2021). The problems are written in natural language and mathematical notation, and their solutions typically involve a sequence of deductions and intermediate calculations.

The questions span seven subjects: prealgebra, algebra, intermediate algebra, precalculus, geometry, number theory, and counting and probability. Each question has a difficulty label from 1 to 5, with 1 denoting the easiest and 5 the hardest problems within a subject. Thus subject and difficulty describe different aspects of the mathematical task.

Each problem comes with a worked reference solution and a final answer. Mathematical expressions are encoded in LaTeX, and diagrams can be represented by Asymptote code. Final answers, such as numbers, fractions or algebraic expressions, are distinguished from the intermediate reasoning and can be checked after accounting for equivalent mathematical forms.

Responses were generated using nine language-model configurations with 4-bit AWQ weight quantization and one non-quantized configuration, Gemma4-E4B, run in FP16. We use abbreviated model names in the figures and result tables; full checkpoint identifiers and precision settings are listed in Appendix A.

Consider the following level-5 number-theory problem from MATH.

Different answers to the same question.

We use Qwen3-8B-AWQ to illustrate three possible observation types for this question: correct completion, incorrect completion, and right censoring at the token limit. Table 1 presents a recorded response for each observation type.

The correct response uses the order restriction, checks the candidate primes and returns 9797 after 1478 tokens. The incorrect response starts with the same restriction but computes the remainder of 62416241 divided by 9797 as 1313 rather than 3333. It consequently rejects 9797 and eventually returns 353353 after 3032 tokens; 353353 is not a divisor of the target number. The censored response tests small primes individually and is still calculating modulo 4343 when its recorded text ends at the cap, without a final answer. This response sample is right-censored at the cap; its natural completion time and eventual correctness remain unobserved.

Differences across model configurations.

Figure 2 extends the same question to ten model configurations, showing three selected responses from each. Each horizontal line represents one response sample, with its length giving the recorded output-token count and its endpoint marking correct completion, incorrect completion or right censoring. The Qwen3-8B lines show the same three responses as Table 1. The selected Gemma4-31B responses finish correctly at shorter lengths, whereas the selected Qwen2.5 responses either finish incorrectly or reach the cap. The examples illustrate variation in both completion length and correctness across configurations and repeated response samples; a longer response need not end in a correct answer.

For a new question, the response and its outcome are unknown before generation. The statistical task is to use the question and configuration to predict the probabilities of correct completion, incorrect completion and remaining unfinished at each budget. Section 3 develops a joint model for those targets.

3 CRATER Framework

CRATER jointly models completion length and correctness using output-token count as the time scale. Correct and incorrect completion are treated as competing events, while responses unfinished at the generation limit are administratively right-censored. The working model combines question features with configuration- and cause-specific time effects, estimated by penalized likelihood.

3.1 Competing risks and token-grid observations

Let XnX_{n} collect the question information and model configuration for record nn. With a common generation limit CC, the observed data are

𝒟={(Xn,T~n,Δn)}n=1N,T~n=min⁡(Tn,C),Δn∈{0,1,2}.\mathcal{D}=\bigl\{(X_{n},\widetilde{T}_{n},\Delta_{n})\bigr\}_{n=1}^{N},\qquad\widetilde{T}_{n}=\min(T_{n},C),\quad\Delta_{n}\in\{0,1,2\}. (4)

Here Δn=1\Delta_{n}=1 denotes the recorded correct completion, Δn=2\Delta_{n}=2 the recorded incorrect completion, and Δn=0\Delta_{n}=0 the administrative right censoring at the generation limit. The numerical representation of the question information is specified in Section 3.2.

Suppose first that completion time TT is continuous. The standard modeling framework for continuous-time competing-risks data, with correct and incorrect completion as the two event types and the generation limit providing administrative right censoring (Putter et al. 2007), can be naturally adopted. Write h¯1\bar{h}_{1} and h¯2\bar{h}_{2} as cause-specific hazards on the original time scale for the two events:

h¯k(t∣X)=limε↓0Pr(t≤T<t+ε,J=k∣T≥t,X)ε,k=1,2.\bar{h}_{k}(t\mid X)=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\frac{\Pr(t\leq T<t+\varepsilon,J=k\mid T\geq t,X)}{\varepsilon},\qquad k=1,2. (5)

Both hazards condition on the response still being unfinished. The survival function of TT is

S¯(t∣X)=exp{−∫0t[h¯1(u∣X)+h¯2(u∣X)]du}.\bar{S}(t\mid X)=\exp\left\{-\int_{0}^{t}[\bar{h}_{1}(u\mid X)+\bar{h}_{2}(u\mid X)]\,du\right\}.

Acomp​(t∣X)=F¯1​(t∣X)F¯1​(t∣X)+F¯2​(t∣X)=F¯1​(t∣X)1−S¯​(t∣X),A_{\mathrm{comp}}(t\mid X)=\frac{\bar{F}_{1}(t\mid X)}{\bar{F}_{1}(t\mid X)+\bar{F}_{2}(t\mid X)}=\frac{\bar{F}_{1}(t\mid X)}{1-\bar{S}(t\mid X)}, (6)

provided the denominator is positive. Thus success within a given budget depends on both the completion probability and the completion-conditioned accuracy.

A type-kk completion contributes density h¯k​(T~n∣Xn)​S¯​(T~n∣Xn)\bar{h}_{k}(\widetilde{T}_{n}\mid X_{n})\bar{S}(\widetilde{T}_{n}\mid X_{n}) to the likelihood, while a censored record contributes S¯​(C∣Xn)\bar{S}(C\mid X_{n}). For independent records, the conditional likelihood is therefore

Lcont=∏n=1N{∏k=12[h¯k​(T~n∣Xn)​S¯​(T~n∣Xn)]𝟏​(Δn=k)​S¯​(C∣Xn)𝟏​(Δn=0)}.L_{\mathrm{cont}}=\prod_{n=1}^{N}\left\{\prod_{k=1}^{2}\bigl[\bar{h}_{k}(\widetilde{T}_{n}\mid X_{n})\bar{S}(\widetilde{T}_{n}\mid X_{n})\bigr]^{\mathbf{1}(\Delta_{n}=k)}\bar{S}(C\mid X_{n})^{\mathbf{1}(\Delta_{n}=0)}\right\}. Each record contributes exactly one survival factor. Only a recorded completion contributes a cause-specific hazard factor.

Although completion lengths are recorded as integer token counts, T~n∈{1,…,C}\widetilde{T}_{n}\in\{1,\ldots,C\}, we use a continuous-time competing-risks model as a working description of completion over the token budget. We evaluate its event densities at the recorded token lengths, retaining ties, and use survival contributions for records coded as administratively censored. This gives the working likelihood

3.2 Model specification

In CRATER, each cause-specific hazard combines question information, a shared time trend and a local time adjustment specific to the model configuration and completion type. With xix_{i} denoting the features extracted from question qiq_{i}, we decompose the normalized hazards for each completion type kk as

hk​(s∣xi,m)=exp⁡{xi⊤​βk⏟question information+c​log⁡s⏟shared time trend+αk​m​(s)⏟local time adjustment},0<s≤1.h_{k}(s\mid x_{i},m)=\exp\left\{\underbrace{x_{i}^{\top}\beta_{k}}_{\text{question information}}+\underbrace{c\log s}_{\text{shared time trend}}+\underbrace{\alpha_{km}(s)}_{\text{local time adjustment}}\right\},\quad 0<s\leq 1. (12)

The first term allows questions to differ, the second describes a common time dependence, and the third allows configurations and completion types to depart from that common trend.

Question information.

The encoder in Section 2.2 supplies information about the problem before a response is generated. For the MATH analysis we use Qwen3-Embedding-8B, which maps each question to zi∈ℝ4096z_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{4096} (Zhang et al. 2025). Directly using all coordinates would introduce a large number of feature coefficients. We therefore seek a low-dimensional representation that retains question information relevant to completion time and correctness.

An exploratory comparison of dimension-reduction methods motivates using linear discriminant analysis (LDA) to obtain a compact representation guided by subject and difficulty labels; Appendix C.1 reports the comparison and its interpretation.

We apply LDA directly to the Qwen embeddings, training separate projections using the difficulty, and subject labels of the training questions. The five difficulty levels yield four discriminant directions, and the seven subjects yield six. Denote the corresponding projection matrices by Vlevel∈ℝ4096×4V_{\mathrm{level}}\in\mathbb{R}^{4096\times 4} and Vsubject∈ℝ4096×6V_{\mathrm{subject}}\in\mathbb{R}^{4096\times 6}. Concatenating these directions gives the ten-dimensional question representation

W=[Vlevel∣Vsubject],ϕ⁡(qi)=W⊤​zi∈ℝ10.W=[V_{\mathrm{level}}\mid V_{\mathrm{subject}}],\qquad\phi(q_{i})=W^{\top}z_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{10}. (13)

We obtain xix_{i} by centering and scaling each coordinate of ϕ⁡(qi)\phi(q_{i}) using training means and standard deviations. Once the projection and scaling parameters are fitted, the transformation requires only a new question’s text. The resulting covariates enter the log hazard through xi⊤​βkx_{i}^{\top}\beta_{k}, with βk\beta_{k} shared across configurations for each completion type kk.

Remark 2 (Question information without dimension reduction).

As an alternative to dimension reduction, we can model the question effect using the standardized original embedding coordinates. Their high dimensionality and potential collinearity can make coefficient estimation unstable and increase the risk of overfitting. For this extension, we add a ridge penalty ρ2​∑k=12‖βk‖22\frac{\rho}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{2}\|\beta_{k}\|_{2}^{2}, with ρ>0\rho>0, to regularize the question coefficients while retaining the same time-effect specification. Section 5.1 examines this extension in routing. Appendix B.3 describes an exact orthogonal reparameterization used for computation.

Shared time trend.

We use log⁡s\log s to provide a parsimonious shared time trend, with the term c​log⁡sc\log s corresponding to a multiplicative factor scs^{c} in the hazard. Together with the piecewise-linear adjustment αk​m​(s)\alpha_{km}(s), this form facilitates computation of the cumulative hazard and likelihood. The adjustment accommodates configuration- and cause-specific departures from the shared trend. Sensitivity to the choice of cc is examined in Appendix C.3.

Local time adjustment.

To allow departures from the shared trend, we use a continuous piecewise-linear function for local time adjustment,

αk​m​(s)=ak​m+bk​m​s+∑j=1Kγk​m​j​(s−κj)+,(v)+=max⁡(v,0).\alpha_{km}(s)=a_{km}+b_{km}s+\sum_{j=1}^{K}\gamma_{kmj}(s-\kappa_{j})_{+},\qquad(v)_{+}=\max(v,0). (14)

The intercept, initial slope, and subsequent slope changes are specific to configuration mm and completion type kk. The main fit uses K=18K=18 candidate knots, placed more densely near the beginning of the observation window; their locations are listed in Appendix C.2. At κj\kappa_{j}, γk​m​j\gamma_{kmj} is the change between the slopes of adjacent intervals. Penalizing ∑j|γk​m​j|\sum_{j}|\gamma_{kmj}| therefore applies the fusion component of the fused lasso to the segment slopes, encouraging neighboring intervals to share the same slope (Tibshirani et al. 2005). Continuity is guaranteed by the hinge basis itself. A nonzero coefficient changes the slope without creating a jump in αk​m\alpha_{km} or the hazard. This construction permits local changes while regularizing their extent, and its estimation is described next. The equivalence to a fused-lasso penalty on adjacent segment slopes is shown in Appendix B.1.

3.3 Penalized likelihood estimation

For fixed cc, substitute (12) into the normalized working likelihood LworkL_{\mathrm{work}}. Write i⁡(n)i(n) and m⁡(n)m(n) for the question and configuration of record nn. The average negative log likelihood is

ℒ⁡(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta) =1N∑n=1N[∑k=12∫0snucexp{xi⁡(n)⊤βk+αk,m⁡(n)(u)}du\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\Bigg[\sum_{k=1}^{2}\int_{0}^{s_{n}}u^{c}\exp\{x_{i(n)}^{\top}\beta_{k}+\alpha_{k,m(n)}(u)\}\,du
−∑k=12𝟏(Δn=k){xi⁡(n)⊤βk+clogsn+αk,m⁡(n)(sn)}].\displaystyle\hskip 40.00006pt-\sum_{k=1}^{2}\mathbf{1}(\Delta_{n}=k)\{x_{i(n)}^{\top}\beta_{k}+c\log s_{n}+\alpha_{k,m(n)}(s_{n})\}\Bigg]. (15)

A censored response sample contributes only the integrated hazards, whereas a completed response sample also contributes its event log hazard. Equal numbers of configurations and repetitions per question give equal question weights in this criterion.

The parameter vector θ\theta collects the feature and spline coefficients. We estimate it by

θ^=arg⁡minθ​{ℒ⁡(θ)+𝒫λ​(θ)},\widehat{\theta}=\arg\min_{\theta}\left\{\mathcal{L}(\theta)+\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}(\theta)\right\}, (16)

where 𝒫λ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda} is the slope-fusion penalty, that is,

𝒫λ​(θ)=λ​∑k,m∑j=1K|γk​m​j|.\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}(\theta)=\lambda\sum_{k,m}\sum_{j=1}^{K}|\gamma_{kmj}|. (17)

The tuning parameter λ\lambda controls changes between adjacent segment slopes. In the LDA specification, the question coefficients βk\beta_{k}, intercepts ak​ma_{km} and initial slopes bk​mb_{km} are unpenalized. This regularizes the complexity of the time adjustments without selecting question features or shrinking their baseline levels. Appendix B.1 discusses the parameterization and optimization.

With the LDA representation fixed, we select λ\lambda by validation within the training sample. All configurations and response samples for a question remain in the same partition, and feature standardization uses only the training questions in each split. After selecting λ\lambda, we refit the model using all training questions and assess its predictions on the separate evaluation sample.

The integrals in (15) are over time, conditional on the question features. On a spline interval the main hazard is u​exp⁡(A+D​u)u\exp(A+Du), whose cumulative integral has an elementary form. Prediction additionally requires integrating S​hkSh_{k}. Numerical quadrature and a proximal Newton method are used for model training, with the objective, derivatives and probability calculations checked independently. Appendix B.2 gives the formulas, optimization checks and tolerances.

4 Empirical Performance

We apply CRATER to the MATH generation data to study how question information and model configuration relate to completion time and correctness. After introducing the evaluation criteria and experimental setup, we report parameter estimates, fitted hazards, and training-sample state probabilities with c=1c=1, followed by ablations of question and token effects.

4.1 Evaluation criteria and experimental setup

Probability evaluation.

We evaluate predicted correct- and incorrect-completion probabilities using the integrated Brier score (IBS), which is commonly used in survival analysis. For normalized budget s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1], define Yn​k​(s)=𝟏​(sn≤s,Δn=k)Y_{nk}(s)=\mathbf{1}(s_{n}\leq s,\Delta_{n}=k) for completion type k=1,2k=1,2. Let ℰ\mathcal{E} denote the set of generation records being evaluated, with Nℰ=|ℰ|N_{\mathcal{E}}=|\mathcal{E}|. Each record corresponds to one response sample. For record nn, let i⁡(n)i(n) be its question index and m⁡(n)m(n) its model-configuration index. We evaluate the mean of the two cause-specific Brier scores and its integral over the observation window:

BS^​(s)\displaystyle\widehat{\operatorname{BS}}(s) =12​Nℰ​∑n∈ℰ∑k=12{F^k​(s∣xi⁡(n),m⁡(n))−Yn​k​(s)}2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N_{\mathcal{E}}}\sum_{n\in\mathcal{E}}\sum_{k=1}^{2}\left\{\widehat{F}_{k}(s\mid x_{i(n)},m(n))-Y_{nk}(s)\right\}^{2}, (18)

At each budget, the Brier score averages the squared differences between predicted completion probabilities and the corresponding binary outcomes, giving equal weight to correct and incorrect completion. IBS averages this probability-prediction error over the normalized budget window. Lower values indicate more accurate probability predictions. We apply the same criterion to training, validation and evaluation records.

To approximate the integral on the token grid, let sj=j/Cs_{j}=j/C for every integer budget j=0,1,…,Cj=0,1,\ldots,C. The trapezoidal approximation is

IBS^≈1C​[BS^​(0)2+∑j=1C−1BS^​(jC)+BS^​(1)2].\widehat{\operatorname{IBS}}\approx\frac{1}{C}\left[\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{BS}}(0)}{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{C-1}\widehat{\operatorname{BS}}\!\left(\frac{j}{C}\right)+\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{BS}}(1)}{2}\right]. (19)

The factor 1/C1/C is the spacing between adjacent normalized budgets. This approximation evaluates the Brier score at every integer token budget and gives equal weight to equal increments of token budget. Since each question has the same numbers of configurations and response samples, the record average also weights questions equally.

The score uses the outcomes of individual response samples. Averaging the ten outcomes before squaring would instead measure error relative to an empirical question-level proportion and would change the criterion. The third state has predicted probability S^=1−F^1−F^2\widehat{S}=1-\widehat{F}_{1}-\widehat{F}_{2}, so the two cause probabilities determine the full three-state prediction. All observed-state indicators follow the cap convention in Section 3.1. Evaluation-sample state-probability curves complement the integrated score in Appendix C.7.

Data partition and working specification.

The analysis includes 2787 questions, with ten model configurations and ten response samples per question–configuration pair. We retain the question partition of 1400 training questions and 1387 evaluation questions. All configurations and response samples of a question remain together in every partition and resample. Thus evaluation concerns predictions for other questions under the same collection of configurations.

The main CRATER specification uses the LDA features in Section 3.2, the shared time term c​log⁡sc\log s, and the continuous piecewise-linear adjustments in (14). We fix c=1c=1 as a convenient working specification. On each spline interval, the hazard then takes the form s​exp⁡(A+D​s)s\exp(A+Ds), with AA and DD constant, and admits an elementary cumulative integral. Sensitivity analyses with alternative values of cc yield similar validation and evaluation scores (Appendix C.3), indicating that predictive performance is insensitive to this choice within the fitted model family. All subsequent analyses use c=1c=1.

The LDA projection is learned from the training questions and held fixed during penalty selection. Within the training sample, we compare candidate values of λ\lambda by validation on questions excluded from training each outcome model. Feature centering and scaling use the training questions in each split. We select the value with the smallest mean validation IBS in (19), and refit on all training questions. Evaluation questions enter neither the LDA fit nor penalty selection.

We use three subject–difficulty-stratified validation splits, each containing 1120 training questions and 280 validation questions. The initial grid contains 19 penalty values from 10−710^{-7} to 10−310^{-3}. A prespecified rule extends a grid boundary by factors of three and ten, for at most two rounds, if the validation minimum occurs there. The time adjustment uses 18 internal knots, held fixed throughout the comparisons.

In the following analysis, evaluation questions are used only to assess the fitted models, not to learn the LDA representation or select penalties. This evaluation set was also examined in earlier experiments.

4.2 Parameter estimates and model fit

We report parameter estimates and model fit results under the specification described above.

Parameter estimates.

Table 2 provides the feature coefficients for correct and incorrect completion, together with their bootstrap standard deviations. The first four coordinates are the LDA directions learned from difficulty labels, and the remaining six are learned from subject labels. Each coordinate is standardized using the training data.

A coefficient βk​j\beta_{kj} is the change in the log hazard of cause-kk associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in feature jj, holding the other features and configuration fixed. The associated hazard ratio is exp⁡(βk​j)\exp(\beta_{kj}). Comparing β1​j\beta_{1j} and β2​j\beta_{2j} shows whether a feature has similar or different associations with the timing of correct and incorrect completion. Their implications for correct-completion probability also depend on both hazards through the survival function.

Table 2 reports the estimated question-feature coefficients and their bootstrap standard deviations. The estimates differ between correct and incorrect completion, suggesting that question features have different associations with the two cause-specific hazards.

Fitted hazards.

Figure 3 displays the fitted cause-specific hazards at centered question features, x=0x=0. Each hazard describes the instantaneous rate of the corresponding completion among responses still unfinished at that budget. The underlying time adjustments appear in Appendix Figure 5.

Correct-completion hazards rise early and then decline across all configurations. Beyond the peak, responses still unfinished have a lower rate of correct completion. Correct completions nevertheless continue to accumulate, so the hazard peak alone does not identify an optimal stopping budget.

Incorrect-completion hazards vary across configurations, with similar patterns within the Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 families. Both Qwen2.5 configurations show a later peak for incorrect than for correct completion, whereas both Qwen3 configurations maintain elevated incorrect-completion hazards at longer budgets. For these configurations and Gemma4-31B, the incorrect-completion hazard eventually exceeds the correct-completion hazard. Qwen3.5, Qwen3.6 and Gemma4-26B retain lower incorrect-completion hazards throughout the plotted positive budgets.

The evaluation results show different patterns of unsuccessful responses across configurations with lower and higher correct-completion rates (Appendix Table 8). The weaker configurations, Qwen2.5 and Qwen3, generally produce shorter responses, and their unsuccessful responses predominantly end in incorrect answers. The stronger configurations, Qwen3.5, Qwen3.6 and Gemma4-26B, generally produce longer responses, and their unsuccessful responses more often exhaust the token budget without completing. Gemma4-31B is a notable exception: it combines the highest correct-completion rate with short responses and few cap hits. These patterns distinguish configurations whose unsuccessful responses mostly end in incorrect answers from those whose unsuccessful responses mostly exhaust the token budget. An overall correct-completion rate does not capture this distinction.

Fitted and observed state probabilities.

Figure 4 compares fitted state probabilities with observed proportions across all 1400 training questions for Gemma4-E4B and Gemma4-31B, using the same fitted model as Figure 3. These configurations illustrate lower and higher overall correct-completion rates, respectively. Solid curves average fitted probabilities over questions; dashed curves give the fractions of response samples completed correctly, completed incorrectly or still unfinished at each token budget.

The fitted curves closely follow the overall completion profiles of both configurations. Correct completions accumulate earlier and reach a higher final proportion for Gemma4-31B, whereas Gemma4-E4B has larger incorrect and unfinished proportions. These pooled comparisons describe in-sample fit; difficulty-specific discrepancies and evaluation-sample diagnostics are reported in Appendices C.6 and C.7.

4.3 Ablation of question and token effects

We examine the question and token effects in model (12) through a complete 2×22\times 2 ablation, retaining or removing each component. The first ablation removes xi⊤​βkx_{i}^{\top}\beta_{k}, retaining the shared log⁡s\log s trend and local adjustment. The second removes both log⁡s\log s and the time-varying part of αk​m​(s)\alpha_{km}(s), giving

hk​(s∣xi,m)=exp⁡{xi⊤​βk+ak​m}.h_{k}(s\mid x_{i},m)=\exp\{x_{i}^{\top}\beta_{k}+a_{km}\}. (20)

This model retains question effects and a separate baseline level for each configuration and completion type, but its hazards are constant over token budget. Its cumulative completion probabilities still increase with the budget through the survival function. The final ablation removes both components, leaving the intercept-only model hk​(s∣m)=exp⁡(ak​m)h_{k}(s\mid m)=\exp(a_{km}). It assigns the same hazards to all questions within a configuration, while retaining separate baseline levels for correct and incorrect completion.

All four models are trained on the same 1400 training questions and scored on both the training and evaluation samples. Each ablation retains the settings of the main specification, with the remaining coefficients reestimated.

Table 3 shows that removing either question effects or token effects increases IBS on both the training and evaluation sets, with larger increases when question effects are removed. On this evaluation sample, CRATER reduces IBS by 6.4% relative to the model without question effects and by 3.0% relative to the model without token effects. Both question information and token-dependent hazards therefore contribute to the observed probability fit and predictive performance. Relative to the intercept-only baseline, either component improves prediction, with question effects yielding the larger reduction in evaluation IBS.

The token-effect ablation removes both the shared trend and the local time adjustment; sensitivity to the shared time coefficient is examined separately in Appendix C.3.

5 Downstream tasks

We consider two downstream applications of CRATER, routing questions to model configurations and token budgets, and predicting success probabilities under repeated sampling.

5.1 Routing before generation

Language-model routing selects a configuration for an incoming question before generating its response, balancing expected answer quality against inference cost. Existing approaches use question information to predict which configuration will perform well: RouteLLM learns from model preferences, RouterBench evaluates nearest-neighbor and neural predictors, and CARROT predicts both performance and cost (Ong et al. 2025; Hu et al. 2024; Somerstep et al. 2025). Budget selection adds a second decision. R2-Router jointly chooses a configuration and an output-length budget using estimated quality–cost curves (Xue et al. 2026). Here we compare nearest-neighbor routing with CRATER-based routing under two question representations, using the same configuration and budget choices within each comparison.

Let a=(m,B)∈𝒜a=(m,B)\in\mathcal{A} denote an action that assigns configuration mm and token cap BB to a question. With a fixed cap, this reduces to choosing a configuration alone. For question features xx, let μa​(x)=μm,B​(x)\mu_{a}(x)=\mu_{m,B}(x) be the probability of correct completion by BB, and let da​(x)=dm,B​(x)d_{a}(x)=d_{m,B}(x) be the expected generation cost. A routing policy specifies the probability πa​(x)\pi_{a}(x) of selecting each action, with πa​(x)≥0\pi_{a}(x)\geq 0 and ∑a∈𝒜πa​(x)=1\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{a}(x)=1. The quality–cost objective is

maxπ⁡𝔼X​[∑a∈𝒜πa​(X)​μa​(X)],𝔼X​[∑a∈𝒜πa​(X)​da​(X)]≤b,\max_{\pi}\ \mathbb{E}_{X}\!\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{a}(X)\mu_{a}(X)\right],\qquad\mathbb{E}_{X}\!\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{a}(X)d_{a}(X)\right]\leq b, (21)

where bb is an average cost allowance. The sums average over the policy’s action probabilities, and 𝔼X\mathbb{E}_{X} averages over the population of incoming questions. For a fixed cost multiplier η≥0\eta\geq 0, maximizing the Lagrangian pointwise gives a deterministic candidate rule

gη​(x)∈arg⁡maxa∈𝒜​{μa​(x)−η​da​(x)}.g_{\eta}(x)\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\{\mu_{a}(x)-\eta d_{a}(x)\}. (22)

Here gη​(x)g_{\eta}(x) returns one model–budget pair, whereas πa​(x)\pi_{a}(x) describes a possibly randomized policy. Larger η\eta gives greater weight to cost. This formulation separates prediction of quality and cost from the allocation decision (Somerstep et al. 2025).

In our setting, quality and cost also depend on when generation is stopped. A response may complete correctly, complete incorrectly, or remain unfinished at its cap. Separate predictions at selected budgets need not correspond to a common completion-time distribution. CRATER supplies that connection through F1F_{1}, F2F_{2} and SS, allowing completed and right-censored records to inform the entire budget range. We evaluate smaller budgets using the recorded responses, assuming that changing the cap leaves the distribution of generated prefixes unchanged under fixed prompts and decoding settings. Success requires a recorded correct completion by the assigned budget; unfinished prefixes are not rescored.

For an action (m,B)(m,B), let pmp_{m} be configuration mm’s price per output token and B≤CB\leq C its allowed budget. The expected number of tokens actually used is Lm(B∣x)=𝔼{min(T,B)∣x,m}L_{m}(B\mid x)=\mathbb{E}\{\min(T,B)\mid x,m\}. Thus CRATER gives

μ^m,B​(x)\displaystyle\widehat{\mu}_{m,B}(x) =F^1​(B/C∣x,m),\displaystyle=\widehat{F}_{1}(B/C\mid x,m),
d^m,B​(x)\displaystyle\widehat{d}_{m,B}(x) =pm​L^m​(B∣x),\displaystyle=p_{m}\widehat{L}_{m}(B\mid x), (23)

where L^m​(B∣x)=C​∫0B/CS^​(s∣x,m)​𝑑s\widehat{L}_{m}(B\mid x)=C\int_{0}^{B/C}\widehat{S}(s\mid x,m)\,ds is the predicted number of output tokens used before completion or the cap BB. Substituting these estimates into (22) gives

g^η​(x)∈arg⁡max(m,B)∈𝒜​{F^1​(B/C∣x,m)−η​pm​L^m​(B∣x)}.\widehat{g}_{\eta}(x)\in\arg\max_{(m,B)\in\mathcal{A}}\left\{\widehat{F}_{1}(B/C\mid x,m)-\eta p_{m}\widehat{L}_{m}(B\mid x)\right\}. (24)

Each value of η\eta defines a candidate rule that selects one action for each question; the final policy is chosen by validation as described below.

Routing methods and question representations.

We compare kk-nearest-neighbor (kkNN) and CRATER predictors in two pairs: one uses the original 4096-dimensional Qwen question embeddings, and the other uses their ten-dimensional LDA representation. A strong reference and a question-independent policy provide common benchmarks.

  1. 1.

    Strong reference. Every question is assigned to Gemma4-31B at the maximum budget CC, selected as the reference by its training correct-completion rate.

  2. 2.

    Zero Router. Adapting the question-independent baseline of Hu et al. (2024), we estimate the correct, incorrect and unfinished proportions and mean cost for each configuration–budget action on the validation questions. A linear program selects fixed probabilities for these actions to minimize mean cost subject to the quality constraints below. Each new question receives one action sampled from this same distribution, without using its content.

  3. 3.

    kkNN. Nearest-neighbor prediction is used for routing in RouterBench and CARROT (Hu et al. 2024; Somerstep et al. 2025). We adapt this approach to configuration–budget actions by averaging correct-by-budget indicators and token consumption over neighboring training questions, converting predicted consumption to cost using the configuration’s token price. We evaluate two versions: one uses the original embeddings with cosine distance, and the other uses the ten-dimensional LDA features with Euclidean distance after coordinate standardization. Each version is compared with CRATER using the corresponding question representation. The predicted success probabilities and costs enter the action-selection rule underlying (24).

  4. 4.

    CRATER. We estimate budget-specific success probabilities and expected costs from the fitted competing-risks distribution via (23) and use these estimates in (24). We consider both the LDA specification in Section 4 and the original-embedding specification with ridge-penalized question coefficients in Remark 2. Training details are provided in Appendix D.1.

Within each representation, both predictors choose a configuration and a budget from the same action set. Their preprocessing and regularization follow their respective training procedures.

Experimental setup.

The candidate actions combine ten configurations with eight caps: 256, 512, 768, 1024, 1536, 2048, 3072, and 4096 tokens. All four question-dependent predictors and Zero Router use these 80 actions. We assign hypothetical prices based on active parameter count and training performance (Table 4). Let AmA_{m} be the active parameter count in billions, using the total count for dense models, and let rmr_{m} rank training full-cap correct-completion rates from lowest to highest. We set qm=(rm−1)/9q_{m}=(r_{m}-1)/9 and pm=Am​(1+qm)p_{m}=A_{m}(1+q_{m}). The capability multiplier ranges from one to two. A response sample assigned cap BB incurs cost pm​min⁡(T~,B)p_{m}\min(\widetilde{T},B); these prices exclude input processing and serving overhead.

All policy choices use validation questions within the training sample. For the experiment, we minimize validation cost subject to quality requirements, rather than fix a cost allowance in (21). Relative to the strong reference, we allow at most a one-percentage-point decrease in correct completion, a half-point increase in incorrect completion, and a one-point increase in unfinished responses. We construct candidate rules from a grid of η\eta values and include the strong-reference rule. A linear program chooses their mixture probabilities to minimize observed validation cost under these constraints. For each new question, the resulting policy samples a rule with the selected probabilities and applies it to the question’s features. The rules and mixture probabilities are held fixed for evaluation. Appendix D.1 gives the grid and selection program. Every evaluation question receives one generation action; offline replay averages over its ten recorded response samples and the policy’s randomization.

Numerical results.

Table 5 reports results within each representation. Zero Router attains 96.42% correct completion and reduces cost by 20.38% relative to the strong reference. With original embeddings, kkNN and CRATER with ridge attain 96.41% and 96.42% correct completion, with cost reductions of 43.95% and 53.39% relative to the reference. CRATER’s cost is 16.83% below kkNN’s.

With LDA features, kkNN and CRATER attain 96.27% and 96.40% correct completion, with cost reductions of 26.98% and 45.19% relative to the reference. CRATER reduces cost by 24.94% relative to kkNN. Thus both within-representation comparisons give lower cost for CRATER-based routing with similar correct-completion point estimates.

All selected policies meet the validation constraints. On evaluation, both kkNN policies and the CRATER-based LDA policy exceed the unfinished-response limit; the LDA kkNN policy also exceeds the correctness-loss limit. Zero Router and the CRATER-based original-embedding policy satisfy the corresponding evaluation constraints at their observed rates.

Cost savings remain stable across capability-based price multipliers when prices reflect differences in active parameter counts. Under a uniform base, both CRATER-based routing versions continue to reduce costs, although the savings are smaller. Across all eight pricing scenarios, the CRATER-based routing versions achieve evaluation correct-completion rates of 94.7%–96.6%, compared with 97.3% for the strong reference (Appendix D.2).

5.2 Predicting model behaviors from repeated sampling

Repeated sampling generates multiple responses to the same question. For question ii and configuration mm, each sample is generated under the same settings and a token budget BB. The quantity pass@kk is the probability that at least one of kk samples completes correctly within its budget, before any subsequent answer-selection step. We predict this probability across token budgets and sample counts using the fitted CRATER model.

Let pi​m​(B)p_{im}(B) be the true single-sample correct-completion probability. Under conditionally independent and identically distributed samples, the standard repeated-success formula is

πi​m(k)​(B)=1−{1−pi​m​(B)}k.\pi_{im}^{(k)}(B)=1-\{1-p_{im}(B)\}^{k}.

It follows because all kk samples fail to complete correctly with probability {1−pi​m​(B)}k\{1-p_{im}(B)\}^{k}. A natural plug-in estimator uses CRATER’s single-sample prediction:

p^i​m​(B)=F^1​(B/C∣xi,m),π^i​m,naive(k)​(B)=1−{1−p^i​m​(B)}k.\widehat{p}_{im}(B)=\widehat{F}_{1}(B/C\mid x_{i},m),\qquad\widehat{\pi}_{im,\mathrm{naive}}^{(k)}(B)=1-\{1-\widehat{p}_{im}(B)\}^{k}.

Directly substituting p^\widehat{p} into 1−(1−p)k1-(1-p)^{k} can yield inaccurate pass@kk predictions because of errors in the predicted single-sample probability and residual variation across questions. We therefore use a beta-binomial model to account for both.

Following the beta-binomial approach of Kazdan et al. (2025) for predicting pass@kk from repeated success counts, we model variation in success probabilities across questions through a beta mixing distribution. We use CRATER’s predicted single-sample success probability to specify the mean of the beta distribution:

Pi​m​(B)|p^i​m​(B)\displaystyle P_{im}(B)\mid\widehat{p}_{im}(B) ∼Beta⁡{μi​m​(B)​ϕm,[1−μi​m​(B)]​ϕm},\displaystyle\sim\operatorname{Beta}\{\mu_{im}(B)\phi_{m},[1-\mu_{im}(B)]\phi_{m}\}, (25)
logit⁡μi​m​(B)\displaystyle\operatorname{logit}\mu_{im}(B) =am+exp⁡(bm)​logit​p^i​m​(B),ϕm>0.\displaystyle=a_{m}+\exp(b_{m})\operatorname{logit}\widehat{p}_{im}(B),\qquad\phi_{m}>0. (26)

The mean link corrects systematic differences between predicted and observed single-sample probabilities through monotone logistic recalibration (Mishra et al. 2022); ϕm\phi_{m} controls the residual variation around that mean. The parameters (am,bm,ϕm)(a_{m},b_{m},\phi_{m}) are shared across budgets within each configuration. Repeated samples on a given question share the same latent probability Pi​m​(B)P_{im}(B) and are independent conditional on it.

We estimate the calibration parameters using a beta-binomial count likelihood based on training-question success counts and their fixed CRATER predictions. Because the same samples contribute counts at multiple budgets, the sum of their marginal log likelihoods is a composite likelihood. Integrating the repeated-success probability over the beta distribution gives

π^i​m(k)​(B)=1−Be⁡{μ^i​m​(B)​ϕ^m,[1−μ^i​m​(B)]​ϕ^m+k}Be⁡{μ^i​m​(B)​ϕ^m,[1−μ^i​m​(B)]​ϕ^m},\widehat{\pi}_{im}^{(k)}(B)=1-\frac{\operatorname{Be}\{\widehat{\mu}_{im}(B)\widehat{\phi}_{m},[1-\widehat{\mu}_{im}(B)]\widehat{\phi}_{m}+k\}}{\operatorname{Be}\{\widehat{\mu}_{im}(B)\widehat{\phi}_{m},[1-\widehat{\mu}_{im}(B)]\widehat{\phi}_{m}\}}, (27)

where Be\operatorname{Be} is the beta function, and μ^i​m​(B)\widehat{\mu}_{im}(B) and ϕ^m\widehat{\phi}_{m} are obtained from the estimated calibration parameters. This prediction averages the repeated-success probability over the conditional beta distribution, incorporating both mean recalibration and residual heterogeneity.

Experimental setup.

We use the CRATER predictor trained in Section 4, keeping its LDA representation, feature scaling, and competing-risks parameters fixed. The beta-binomial parameters are estimated using all ten samples for each of the 1400 training questions and each configuration, together with their fixed single-sample predictions at budgets 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, and 4096. The two stages thus use the same training questions. We then evaluate repeated-success predictions on the separate set of 1387 evaluation questions. Appendix E.1 gives the calibration details.

We assess the predictions on the 1387 evaluation questions, using their ten samples as an empirical reference. For question ii and configuration mm, let Di​m​(B)D_{im}(B) count correct completions within budget BB among RR evaluation samples. The empirical pass@kk estimator is

pass​@⁡k^i​m(B)=1−(R−Di​m​(B)k)(Rk),k=1,…,R,\widehat{\operatorname{pass@}k}_{im}(B)=1-\frac{\binom{R-D_{im}(B)}{k}}{\binom{R}{k}},\qquad k=1,\ldots,R, (28)

where the numerator is zero when R−Di​m​(B)<kR-D_{im}(B)<k (Chen et al. 2021). Under conditional iid sampling, this estimates the probability of at least one success in kk samples. We compare predictions with these estimates for k=1,…,10k=1,\ldots,10.

Table 6 compares the naive plug-in and beta-binomial predictions with the empirical estimates at k=5k=5 and k=10k=10. Both predictions use the same single-sample predictor, so their comparison assesses mean recalibration and beta mixing jointly. Appendix Table 14 reports the complete results for k=1,…,10k=1,\ldots,10 at all six budgets, including the token-effect ablation below.

Calibration brings the predicted mean pass@10 closer to the empirical estimates at every reported budget. At 512 tokens, for example, the naive plug-in prediction is 0.901, compared with 0.521 after calibration and an empirical estimate of 0.514.

Token-effect ablation.

To examine whether modeling completion time remains useful after beta-binomial calibration, we use the constant-hazard ablation in (20). It removes both the shared log⁡s\log s trend and the time-varying local adjustment, retaining question effects and configuration- and cause-specific intercepts. The remaining coefficients are reestimated, and a separate beta-binomial layer is trained using the same 1400 questions, ten samples per question–configuration pair and six budgets as for CRATER. Thus both models receive the same calibration procedure.

Table 7 compares the calibrated mean pass@10 predictions with the empirical estimates. Across the 60 budget–kk combinations in Appendix Table 14, the average absolute difference between predicted and empirical mean pass@kk is 0.00887 for CRATER and 0.06433 without token effects. Thus, the shared beta-binomial calibration used here does not fully compensate for the removal of token effects.

At the 4096-token budget, CRATER’s predicted mean pass@10 is 1.9 percentage points below the empirical estimate. The model without token effects is closer to the empirical estimate at this budget, although CRATER performs better across budgets overall. Appendix E.3 shows that relaxing the calibration model’s parameter sharing across budgets brings mean pass@10 closer to the empirical estimate using the same single-sample predictions from CRATER. This sensitivity analysis helps explain the maximum-budget result, although the more flexible calibration can produce predictions that decrease as the budget increases.

6 Discussion

CRATER jointly models completion time and correctness to assess language-model responses under token-budget constraints. The competing-risks formulation distinguishes the probabilities of correct completion, incorrect completion, and remaining unfinished throughout the observed budget range. Expected token consumption follows from the same distribution, connecting the quality of an answer to the resources needed to obtain it. This common structure allows completed and censored responses to contribute to estimation and supplies consistent probability targets for different generation decisions. Its practical value lies in using one fitted model to describe response behavior and support subsequent resource allocation.

The empirical analysis shows that both question information and token effects contribute to prediction. Their roles are complementary: question features describe differences between problems, while token effects describe how completion rates vary with the token budget. The fitted hazards further reveal distinct patterns for correct and incorrect completion across configurations. In particular, a declining correct-completion hazard indicates that responses still unfinished have a lower rate of correct completion as the budget increases, even though cumulative success can continue to rise. Overall accuracy and average response length do not show how correct- and incorrect-completion rates change with the token budget. CRATER describes these changes separately for each completion type and model configuration.

The two important downstream applications illustrate how this distribution can inform different decisions. Routing uses predicted success and expected consumption to select a configuration and budget before generation. The comparisons with nearest-neighbor predictors show lower costs under the primary price assumptions, although savings depend on relative token prices and validation constraints need not hold on evaluation questions. Most selected actions retain the full cap, so these results do not isolate the benefit of budget selection. Repeated-sampling prediction uses the single-attempt probabilities as inputs to a beta-binomial model that adjusts their mean and accounts for residual heterogeneity. The resulting average pass@kk predictions agree more closely with empirical estimates than direct plug-in predictions.

The current analysis has several limitations. The empirical evaluation focuses on mathematical reasoning tasks with verifiable answers under fixed generation settings. Extending the framework to open-ended tasks would require a clearly defined criterion for successful completion and a reliable way to assess it. The model also uses only question information, completion lengths and observed outcomes; it does not incorporate token-level log probabilities produced during decoding. These signals may contain additional information about the evolving response and could support updated predictions as generation proceeds. Because they become available during generation, their use would extend the present prediction setting to decisions informed by a partially generated response.

Future work could improve question representations and test the framework on new tasks, model configurations, and independently collected responses. Evaluating the routing strategies under actual serving costs would also help assess their practical value. Incorporating information observed during decoding could also support decisions on whether to continue an attempt or start another. Speculative decoding, in which a smaller model proposes tokens that a target model verifies (Leviathan et al. 2023), offers another setting for studying completion probabilities together with the computational costs of drafting and verification. Finally, adding majority voting or verifier-based answer selection would change the target from obtaining at least one correct response to returning a correct selected answer. Modeling that selection step would connect the present framework more directly to the outcome delivered to a user.
